author: eagleholly1
title: Love this game…sometimes!
content:
Candy Crush is a fun game to play…initially.  It is easy to  if learn and has great graphics.  Early levels are easy to pass, and the steady flow of wins is what hooks us.
But the level of difficulty increases quickly, time required to complete the levels can be absurdly long, and interest begins to lag.  And of course these things are controlled by the game’s program.  But by this time we’re hooked, and so play on.  Some of the more generous rewards (that allow you to keep playing) are probably impossible to achieve unless you pay to play.  For example, each level shows a string of boosters you can achieve if you complete 5 levels without failing. If you fail any level you have to go back to the beginning—not just complete that level and then continue on.
I find myself looking for other games that are not as punitive as Candy Crush can be, and have been playing those more frequently instead.

author: TheTheory
content: I never really gave Candy Crush a fair shake before. Back when it first released it was easy to pan as a knockoff of its jeweled cousin, not to mention being a go-to example of the evils of free-to-pay, in-app purchases, timers, currencies, etc, etc, at a time when all of those things—so commonplace now—were seen as the downfall of mobile gaming (and perhaps gaming without the qualifier). We probably weren’t wrong for our fears—like I said, these elements are a given in most free-to-play today—but it’s weird coming back to Candy Crush and seeing how forgiving their brand of free-to-play is. Gaming developers have seriously clamped down hard on free-to-play, such that any actual fun is hidden behind break-out-your-wallet IAPs—usually within the first hour or two. I’ve played two days of Candy Crush without impediment to the fun. And let me tell you, if matching pieces of candy and watching them pop sounds like fun, Candy Crush delivers. Few things are as satisfying as setting off a huge chain reaction that clears the board. It’s visually gratifying, and makes grinding some of the harder levels worthwhile. Because, yes, there will be some grinding. The only criticism I can levy at Candy Crush is that there is a huge element of luck involved. This luck comes in two forms: 1. Your opening board’s randomized candy layout. 2. How big your ending cascades end up being. You can have a perfect strategy (or multiple strategies), but because of the amount of randomization, you can fail a level over, and over, and over, until you finally get an ideal opening board and/or ending chain. That’s frustrating. Then again, luck is a part of a lot of games. I remember flinging birds at pigs, and I could stretch that stupid slingshot the same way each time and get a different result. C’est la vie. To whatever extent you like your match 3 genre games candy coated and puzzle oriented, Candy Crush remains surprisingly relevant.

author: Petalmist <(^-^<)
title: Played for Years
content:
I’ve played Candy Crush on and off for a few years now. From my perspective of things, complaints/suggestions by other reviewers have since been fixed. 

In the past, the only way to get gold bars was to pay. If you didn’t have gold bars, you couldn’t buy boosters at will, and would have to deal all the cards dealt, even if they were virtually impossible without boosters if you needed a certain kind but didn’t have them. This would personally result in me not playing for weeks, as well as only having a total of five gold bars in the span of three years. However, you can now get gold bars depending on how fast you complete groupings of levels, and whether you did it above or below the average speed of other players. It helps gameplay very much and speeds it up, so to speak. 

Additionally, just a year or two ago Candy Crush added milestones. These give out small bundles of awards which include a restoration of health, discounted bundles you can buy, etc. I just reached level 1,000 and was pleasantly surprised with what would otherwise be known as a mini ‘jackpot’ without having to spin the prize wheel. I also love the mini events and challenges: the mini storylines, booster-rewards,..

Overall, Candy Crush is a great, aesthetically pleasing game. It’s not necessarily as addictive as more recent games due to less surprises and suspense, but I can’t imagine Candy Crush with any suspense at all. I love Candy Crush, as Candy Crush. I look forward to playing a lot more in the future.

author: Pykamun
title: From my go-to game to a frustrating pay-to-pass experience
content:
I’ve played Candy Crush for years. It used to be my go-to game because it was simple, relaxing, and still required enough strategy to keep it interesting. Unfortunately, over time it has started to feel less like a puzzle game and more like a game designed to push you into spending money.

I understand difficult levels. What I don’t understand are levels where the objective compared to the number of moves given feels practically impossible unless you use boosters or buy additional moves. Difficulty also doesn’t seem to progress logically. A much earlier level can suddenly be dramatically harder than levels hundreds of stages later, which makes the difficulty feel manufactured rather than part of a natural progression.

What frustrates me even more is how unpredictable some of the mechanics have become. For example, fish will sometimes ignore an obvious target needed to complete the level and instead hit something completely irrelevant, or even interfere with a combination or strategy I was setting up. At that point, it stops feeling like my decisions determine whether I win.

I’ve also noticed that once you start spending money, it seems like you are constantly being put in situations where you need to spend again. When passing one level can come down to buying gold bars just to get the extra moves necessary to finish it, the game stops being fun.

After years of playing, I’m uninstalling it. I don’t mind paying occasionally for a game I enjoy, but I don’t want to feel like paying has become practically necessary just to continue playing. Candy Crush used to be relaxing. Now it is frustrating enough that it has made me dislike a game I genuinely enjoyed for years.

One star because a game should make me want to play another level, not make me feel like I need to pull out my credit card to finish one.

author: Don Coyote -><-
title: Better have $$$
content: I’ve been playing this for years, and gotten very far. So many of the levels for a while now are just about impossible to beat, now, without buying the extra powers or enough “coins” to continue a level after you’ve used up all the moves. Just to advance in this game, you need to spend a LOT, or have infinite patience and keep playing a level over and over until the layout randomly changes to a very lucky one. Almost everything the game used to provide you with to help with (overly) difficult levels gets modified to make it less useful. Like, they used to give you more and more turns to play each time you lost a level - you’d still have to use coins (which are rarely attainable unless you pay real money) to use all the extra moves - but now, instead, is a “random” wheel after each lost that gives you only a few extra moves, and they do not accumulate. As for the “random” gifts still in the game, I could be wrong, but they seem to be calibrated to give lousy gifts way more often - the “random” layouts at the start of the each level likewise seem to form more difficult patterns than easier ones. I’m tired of having to pay to play this game after all this time. I’ve quit for a while before, but I am truly thinking of erasing this from my phone for good. The impossible levels are not so fun after a few dozen tries, and I don’t want to keep throwing away three to five dollars just to get thru each one.

author: Blukaka
title: Not fun anymore
content:
I’ve been playing this game for two years, and the early experience was great. The levels were fun, the 15‑level cycles were motivating, and weekly tournaments and events felt rewarding. I enjoyed progressing without spending real money — using bonuses, boosters, and watching ads was enough.

However, once I reached around level 15,000, the difficulty changed dramatically. Levels became nearly impossible to pass without extra moves, boosters stopped helping, and winning any event or competition became unrealistic. Progress now depends almost entirely on getting 20+ extra moves from the Wheel of Fortune.

At higher levels, the game no longer feels enjoyable or fair. It’s frustrating, repetitive, and seems designed to push players toward spending real money. After reaching the 20,000+ range, it feels like there’s nothing meaningful left to offer.

Unfortunately, I’m quitting.

author: Evo57!!!
title: Cash grabbing charlatans
content:
Candy Crush Saga isn’t a puzzle game. It’s a monetization engine disguised as one.

Almost every aspect of the game feels carefully designed to push you into spending money. The visuals, sounds, constant pop-ups, limited-time offers, races against other players, and endless prompts to buy boosters all create pressure to pay rather than simply enjoy playing.

Some levels don’t feel challenging because of skill. They feel deliberately designed to make you run out of moves so you’re tempted to buy extra ones or purchase boosters. It’s incredibly frustrating when success seems to depend more on your wallet than your ability.

The timed competitions are another example. They encourage players to spend money just to keep up, turning what should be a casual game into a race driven by purchases rather than enjoyment.

My biggest concern is how this affects younger or more vulnerable players. The game is full of psychological nudges that encourage spending, and I would strongly advise parents not to let children play it if they have access to payment methods.

There are plenty of genuinely enjoyable puzzle games that reward strategy and skill. In my opinion, this isn’t one of them. It feels designed first and foremost to maximize spending.

I can’t recommend it. One star.
